aesop-001.title: The Fox and the Grapes
aesop-001.lead: A hungry fox spotted a bunch of grapes hanging high on a trellis and did his best to reach them by jumping as high as he could.
aesop-001.body_html: A hungry fox spotted a bunch of grapes hanging high on a trellis and did his best to reach them by jumping as high as he could. Time after time he jumped, straining his muscles to the limit, but it was all in vain; the grapes hung just a little too high. Finally, hot and tired, he gave up trying. As he walked away with his head held high, he remarked to himself, "I thought those grapes were ripe, but I see now they are quite sour." It is easy to despise what we cannot have.

aesop-002.title: The Lion and the Mouse
aesop-002.lead: A mighty lion lay sleeping in the forest when a tiny mouse accidentally ran across his face and woke him.
aesop-002.body_html: A mighty lion lay sleeping in the forest when a tiny mouse accidentally ran across his face and woke him. The lion seized the frightened little creature and was about to swallow him when the mouse cried out, "Please, mighty lion, let me go! If you do, I promise I shall never forget your kindness. Perhaps one day I may be able to return the favor." The lion, amused by this promise, let the mouse go. Some time later, the lion was caught in a hunter's net. As he roared in rage and struggled futilely, the little mouse heard his voice. She ran to the net and began gnawing the ropes with her teeth, working as hard as she could. Soon the lion was free! "You see," said the mouse, "even a mouse can help a lion.

aesop-003.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
aesop-003.lead: A thirsty crow found a pitcher with a little water in it, but the water was too low for her to reach with her beak.
aesop-003.body_html: A thirsty crow found a pitcher with a little water in it, but the water was too low for her to reach with her beak. She tried time and again but could not drink. Then she had an idea. Picking up small pebbles, she dropped them one by one into the pitcher. With each pebble the water level rose a little higher. At last the water was high enough for her to drink. She quenched her thirst and flew away. In a pinch a good use of our wits may help us out.

aesop-004.title: The Dog and the Shadow
aesop-004.lead: A dog crossed a bridge carrying a piece of meat in his mouth.
aesop-004.body_html: A dog crossed a bridge carrying a piece of meat in his mouth. Looking down at the water below, he saw his own reflection. He thought it was another dog with a piece of meat, and he wanted that meat too. So he snapped at the reflection in the water. But when he opened his mouth to bite, his own piece of meat fell into the water and was lost. The greedy dog lost everything by being dissatisfied with what he had.

aesop-005.title: The North Wind and the Sun
aesop-005.lead: The north wind and the sun disputed as to which was the stronger of the two.
aesop-005.body_html: The north wind and the sun disputed as to which was the stronger of the two. At last they agreed to settle the matter by a test. They would see which of them could get a traveler to remove his cloak. The north wind tried first. He blew hard and cold, and the stronger he blew, the more closely the traveler wrapped his cloak about himself. Then the sun tried. He came out warm and bright, and the traveler soon felt the warmth and unfastened his cloak. A gentle manner is often more powerful than force.

aesop-006.title: The Tortoise and the Eagle
aesop-006.lead: A tortoise, envying the birds their ability to fly, begged an eagle to teach him.
aesop-006.body_html: A tortoise, envying the birds their ability to fly, begged an eagle to teach him. The eagle protested that it was impossible; a tortoise had no wings. But the tortoise persisted until finally the eagle, tired of his importuning, took him up to a great height and released him. Down, down, down fell the tortoise, and he was dashed upon the rocks below. Nature is not to be changed by wishing.

indian-001.title: The Lion and the Crane
indian-001.lead: A crane once removed a bone stuck in a lion's throat, having carefully inserted his beak and extracted the bone.
indian-001.body_html: A crane once removed a bone stuck in a lion's throat, having carefully inserted his beak and extracted the bone. The grateful lion promised him the greatest reward. However, when the crane ventured to claim his payment, the lion replied, "What more do you want? I have spared your life; is not that payment enough?" The crane flew away, realizing that there is no trust among the ungrateful and that good deeds done to the wicked often go unrewarded. Ingratitude is the mark of the base and disloyal.

indian-002.title: The Lambikin
indian-002.lead: A lamb, meeting a jackal, made an agreement to wait until he grew fatter.
indian-002.body_html: A lamb, meeting a jackal, made an agreement to wait until he grew fatter. This he repeated with every creature that sought to devour him. When at last pursued for real, he fled to his mother's house. From inside a drum made of his brother's skin, the lamb spoke to each pursuer with a riddle. The jackal, the wolf, and the tiger each failed to answer and departed. But when the jackal returned with the answer, he tore open the drum and devoured the lamb. Cunning alone, without courage, may not always avail against determined enemies.

indian-003.title: The Cruel Crane Outwitted
indian-003.lead: A wicked crane told the fish in a drying pond that he would carry them to a larger body of water.
indian-003.body_html: A wicked crane told the fish in a drying pond that he would carry them to a larger body of water. One by one he would fly them to a distant tree, where he killed and ate them. The fish agreed, and the crane transported them, feasting on each. When a crab agreed to be transported, it gripped the crane's neck tightly, demanding to know where the others had gone. Learning of the crane's treachery, the crab killed him by cutting through his neck as he flew, and they both fell into the water. Though cunning is powerful, loyalty and courage overcome even the most deceptive schemes.

grimm-001.title: Hansel and Gretel
grimm-001.lead: A poor woodcutter's two children are abandoned in the forest to avoid starvation.
grimm-001.body_html: A poor woodcutter's two children are abandoned in the forest to avoid starvation. Hansel, having overheard his parents' plan, fills his pockets with white pebbles that shine like silver in the moonlight, allowing the children to follow them home. When abandoned again, they use breadcrumbs as markers, but birds eat the trail. Deep in the forest, they discover a cottage made entirely of gingerbread, belonging to a cannibalistic witch. She imprisons Hansel to fatten him for eating. Clever Gretel pushes the witch into her own oven and frees her brother. They escape with treasures and jewels, eventually reuniting with their father, whose cruel stepmother has died. All their sorrows ended, and they lived in comfort and joy.

grimm-002.title: Little Snow White
grimm-002.lead: A beautiful princess, Snow White, is born to a king and queen.
grimm-002.body_html: A beautiful princess, Snow White, is born to a king and queen. When the queen dies, the king remarries a vain woman who consults a magic mirror daily, believing herself the fairest in the land. When the mirror reveals that Snow White surpasses her beauty, the jealous queen orders a huntsman to kill the girl. Snow White flees into the forest and finds refuge with seven dwarfs. The queen, discovering this through her mirror, disguises herself and gives Snow White a poisoned apple. The girl falls into deathlike sleep. The dwarfs place her in a glass coffin. A passing prince, struck by her beauty, kisses her and awakens her. Snow White and the prince are married, and the queen, learning the news, falls from her castle to her death in rage and despair.

grimm-003.title: The Goose-Girl
grimm-003.lead: A princess is sent to marry a distant prince, accompanied by her mother's magical lock of hair for protection.
grimm-003.body_html: A princess is sent to marry a distant prince, accompanied by her mother's magical lock of hair for protection. During the journey, her waiting-maid wickedly overpowers her, steals her identity, and forces the true princess into servitude as a goose-girl. The prince, deceived, accepts the false bride. A talking horse's head, hanging on the city gate, begins to converse with the true princess, revealing her identity through their conversations. The king, moved by the story, determines the deception. The false bride is condemned to die in a barrel filled with nails and rolling oil. The true princess marries the prince, and they live happily.

grimm-004.title: The Valiant Little Tailor
grimm-004.lead: A poor tailor kills seven flies with a single blow of his hand.
grimm-004.body_html: A poor tailor kills seven flies with a single blow of his hand. Boasting of this feat, he creates a belt reading "SEVEN AT ONE BLOW," intending to deceive the world into thinking he slew seven men. Giants and the king believe this exaggeration and hire him as a warrior, fearing his supposed prowess. Through clever wit rather than strength, the tailor defeats all challengers—catching one giant under a bridge, making another jealous until he crushes himself, and outwitting all who oppose him. Finally, the king offers him his daughter's hand in marriage and a kingdom as reward. The boastful tailor becomes a great lord, and his valor is spoken of throughout the land.

grimm-005.title: The Wolf and the Seven Young Kids
grimm-005.lead: A mother goat warns her seven kids about a dangerous wolf, describing his rough voice and black feet as identifying features before she leaves to gather food.
grimm-005.body_html: A mother goat warns her seven kids about a dangerous wolf, describing his rough voice and black feet as identifying features before she leaves to gather food. The wolf arrives and attempts deception three times. The kids recognize his rough voice and refuse entry. The wolf consumes chalk to soften his voice and tricks a miller into whitening his paw with flour. When he returns, the kids request proof. Seeing his white paw, they open the door. The wolf devours six kids; only the youngest survives by hiding in the clock case. The mother goat discovers the devastation. Finding the sleeping wolf in a meadow with movement in his belly, she cuts him open, freeing all six kids unharmed. She fills his stomach with stones and stitches him closed. When the wolf awakens and attempts to drink from a well, the heavy stones pull him down to his drowning.

russian-001.title: The Sorry Drunkard
russian-001.lead: An intoxicated man drowns crossing a river during a storm.
russian-001.body_html: An intoxicated man drowns crossing a river during a storm. His son, Petrúsha, encounters the Devil disguised as a handsome youth on the road. The Devil reveals that Petrúsha's father has been transformed into a beast of burden as punishment for his drunkenness. A kind maiden helps guide Petrúsha. Using a sacred cross, Petrúsha breaks the enchantment and recovers his father, who is restored to human form and renounces drink forever. The family is reunited in gratitude and redemption, and Petrúsha marries the kind maiden who helped him.

russian-002.title: The Wolf and the Tailor
russian-002.lead: Christ commands a hungry wolf to eat various animals to satisfy his hunger.
russian-002.body_html: Christ commands a hungry wolf to eat various animals to satisfy his hunger. The wolf attempts to devour a horse but is kicked and crippled. He next attacks a cow but is gored. A boar wounds him in the leg. Finally, a clever tailor encounters the predator on the road. The tailor, pretending to measure the wolf for clothing, uses the wolf's tail as a whip and beats him savagely. Seven wolves pursuing the tailor up a tree abandon their pursuit when they see their leader without a tail. The tailless wolf's cowardice saves the tailor's life, and he escapes to the city, becoming renowned for his bold encounter.

russian-003.title: Egorí the Brave and the Gipsy
russian-003.lead: A struggling gipsy seeks divine guidance from Egorí the Brave through prayer and fasting.
russian-003.body_html: A struggling gipsy seeks divine guidance from Egorí the Brave through prayer and fasting. God reveals to Egorí that the gipsy's trade is deception and theft, and instructs him to tell the gipsy that his livelihood is evil. When Egorí conveys this message, the gipsy asks to retrieve his stirrup from Egorí's pocket. Egorí discovers his pocket empty—he has been robbed. The prophecy proves immediately true. The gipsy, freed from moral constraint by this divine revelation, pursues increasingly elaborate confidence schemes and cons, becoming a legendary rogue of the steppes.

russian-004.title: A Tale of the Dead (Corpse Returns)
russian-004.lead: A peasant encounters a risen corpse that terrorizes a village, killing the inhabitants one by one.
russian-004.body_html: A peasant encounters a risen corpse that terrorizes a village, killing the inhabitants one by one. Through investigation, the peasant learns the methods by which the dead are revived and discovers counter-magic for healing. He saves two young villagers from the corpse's grasp through magical intervention. The peasant determines that a sorcerer in a distant cottage has raised the dead through dark ritual. The village community unites to destroy the sorcerer by ritual burning, and the corpse falls lifeless. The peasant becomes a hero, celebrated throughout the region for his courage and knowledge of the old magic.

persian-001.title: Zal and the Simurgh
persian-001.lead: In the land of Seistan there ruled a mighty lord named Saum, girt with power and glory, yet his heart was heavy, for he had no son to follow him.
persian-001.body_html: In the land of Seistan there ruled a mighty lord named Saum, girt with power and glory, yet his heart was heavy, for he had no son to follow him. At last a child was born to him, but the infant's hair was white as that of an aged man. Saum looked upon this wonder with horror, fearing the mockery of the nobles, and in his anger he commanded his servants to carry the babe to Mount Alberz and abandon him there to die. The great bird Simurgh, who nested upon that mountain, found the crying infant and bore him to her eyrie, meaning to feed him to her young. But pity stirred within her, and she raised the child as her own, and moons and years rolled above their heads until the babe was grown to be a youth full of strength and beauty. Then it came to pass that Saum dreamed a dream, in which a rider rebuked him bitterly for abandoning his own blood. Fear came upon him for his sin, and he journeyed to the mountain and called upon God. The Simurgh brought the youth, whom men now called Zal, down to his father. When Saum beheld his son, his heart rejoiced within him, and he embraced him, and entreated his forgiveness.

persian-002.title: Zohak and the Blacksmith's Banner
persian-002.lead: There dwelt in Arabia a king named Zohak, tempted by the demon Ahriman to slay his own father and seize the throne.
persian-002.body_html: There dwelt in Arabia a king named Zohak, tempted by the demon Ahriman to slay his own father and seize the throne. Ahriman, disguised as a cook, kissed Zohak upon each shoulder, and from that kiss sprang two hissing black serpents that could not be cut away. The demon counseled Zohak that the serpents required the brains of men for their nourishment, and so daily were two men slaughtered to feed them, and Zohak reigned in terror for a thousand years. Among his subjects was a blacksmith named Kaveh, whose sons had already been taken to feed the serpents. When Zohak's officers brought him a false declaration praising the tyrant's justice and commanded him to sign it, Kaveh refused. "I will not lend my hand unto this lie," he cried, and seized the declaration and tore it to fragments, scattering them into the air before the whole court. Then Kaveh tore off the leathern apron that blacksmiths wear to guard their knees, and raised it aloft upon a lance as a banner, and the people, seeing his defiance, rose up behind him against Zohak's tyranny.

persian-003.title: The Fall of Jamshid
persian-003.lead: Jamshid reigned as king over the land for seven hundred years, girt with such might that the very spirits of the air obeyed him.
persian-003.body_html: Jamshid reigned as king over the land for seven hundred years, girt with such might that the very spirits of the air obeyed him. He founded the city of Persepolis and established the feast of Nowruz, and beneath his rule the people knew neither sickness nor want. But as the years passed, the heart of Jamshid was uplifted in pride, and he forgot whence came his weal and the source of his blessings. He beheld only himself upon the earth, and in his arrogance he named himself God, and sent forth his own image to be worshipped. At once his glory departed from him. The kings and nobles of the land rose up against him, and the armies of Arabia and Persia marched to overthrow him. Jamshid fled before their advance, but the serpent-king Zohak hunted him to the ends of the earth, and there was no refuge left for the king who had forgotten his maker.

native-001.title: Moowis (The Dirt-and-Rag Man)
native-001.lead: A young man, rejected and wounded by the scorn of a beautiful girl he loves, seeks supernatural aid in his despair.
native-001.body_html: A young man, rejected and wounded by the scorn of a beautiful girl he loves, seeks supernatural aid in his despair. Through magic, he constructs a being named Moowis from discarded materials—rags, bark, dirt, and refuse—molding them into an attractive stranger. This created being, through enchantment, appears beautiful and charming. Moowis successfully wins the girl's heart, and she pursues him eagerly after their marriage. As dawn approaches, the sun's warmth begins to decompose the magical being. The girl discovers that her new husband dissolves into scattered clothing and bones, the very materials from which he was made. She learns too late that appearance without substance is worthless, and her selfish rejection has cost her true happiness.

native-002.title: The Boy Who Snared the Sun
native-002.lead: A small boy becomes enraged when the sun damages his precious birdskin coat during the day's travel.
native-002.body_html: A small boy becomes enraged when the sun damages his precious birdskin coat during the day's travel. Vowing revenge against the celestial body, he fasts for many days to gain spiritual power. His sister, taking pity, provides him with a magical cord. Before dawn, the boy climbs a mountain and snares the sun as it rises, trapping it in the cord and plunging the world into darkness. All creatures suffer in perpetual night—the hunt fails, plants wither, and animals freeze. Finally, the dormouse, largest animal on earth, volunteers to sacrifice itself to free the sun. It charges at the magical snare and breaks it with its strength, freeing the sun and rescuing the world. But the effort diminishes the dormouse forever, reducing it to a tiny creature.

Twist Span: He fasts and gains spiritual power. His sister provides him with a magical cord. He snares the sun as it rises, plunging the world into darkness.

native-003.title: A Legend of Manabozho
native-003.lead: Manabozho grieves deeply when his adopted wolf-son is killed in a lake by water spirits.
native-003.body_html: Manabozho grieves deeply when his adopted wolf-son is killed in a lake by water spirits. In his rage, he kills the spirit chiefs responsible for the death. But the spirits retaliate by causing a devastating flood that rises over the earth, threatening all life. Manabozho prays for salvation and receives help from diving animals. A muskrat dives to the depths and retrieves a small bit of earth from the bottom of the primordial waters. Using sacred dust and the earth brought by the muskrat, Manabozho spreads the material across the waters, creating land. From this act, the world is restored and renewed, and the cycle of life continues. The tale teaches that from grief and loss can come creation and renewal.
characteristics: Culture/Region: Native America (Anishinaabe)

native-004.title: The Girl Who Married the Pine-Tree
native-004.lead: A beautiful girl escapes an arranged marriage by fleeing into a sacred grove of ancient pines where forest sprites are said to dwell.
native-004.body_html: A beautiful girl escapes an arranged marriage by fleeing into a sacred grove of ancient pines where forest sprites are said to dwell. In the forest's depths, she hears a voice—tender and devoted—offering her marriage to the pine tree itself. The voice promises eternal protection and love beneath its branches. The girl accepts this union, speaking vows to the ancient tree. From that day forward, she vanishes into the forest depths. Occasionally, hunters passing through the grove at sunset glimpse a maiden dancing gracefully with a handsome youth among the trees, only to vanish when approached. It is said she dances with the spirit of the pine tree she married, forever happy in her choice to escape mortal convention.
characteristics: Culture/Region: Native America

native-005.title: The Spirits and the Lovers
native-005.lead: A chief's daughter loves a weak and unproven young warrior named Karkapaha, rejecting all powerful suitors.
native-005.body_html: A chief's daughter loves a weak and unproven young warrior named Karkapaha, rejecting all powerful suitors. The chief, outraged by this choice, orders the youth's execution. Before the sentence can be carried out, the couple flees to the Hill of Little Spirits seeking sanctuary. The spirits, impressed by the couple's devotion, intervene on their behalf. They kill the pursuing warriors and grant Karkapaha a new spirit of great strength and prowess. Transformed into a formidable warrior of legendary power, Karkapaha returns to his chief. He displays feats of incredible strength, lifting boulders and breaking weapons. Witnessing this transformation, the chief relents and accepts the marriage, declaring that the spirits' blessing has proven Karkapaha worthy. The couple marries and lives in honor.

irish-001.title: Frank Martin and the Fairies
irish-001.lead: A weaver named Frank Martin begins to suffer from fairy visions that afflict his mind.
irish-001.body_html: A weaver named Frank Martin begins to suffer from fairy visions that afflict his mind. He claims to maintain "the most friendly intimacy" with the small creatures inhabiting his workshop, creatures no one else can perceive. They speak to him constantly in elaborate conversations, offering advice and companionship. His neighbors believe him mad, yet Frank insists his fairy friends have "baptized him against them"—protected him through magical means. Frank seems content in his condition, never troubled or frightened. He works at his loom while conversing freely with invisible companions, and his contentment brings him peace that ordinary folk never know. His unusual gift transforms what might be madness into a peculiar form of happiness.
characteristics: Culture/Region: Ireland

irish-002.title: The Priest's Supper
irish-002.lead: A fisherman named Dermod encounters fairies by a river who engage him in conversation.
irish-002.body_html: A fisherman named Dermod encounters fairies by a river who engage him in conversation. They ask him to pose a theological question to Father Horrigan: Do fairies possess immortal souls deserving salvation? Dermod agrees and brings the query to the priest. Father Horrigan, rather than dismissing the question, boldly invites the fairies to ask him directly about their souls' salvation. When word reaches the fairy folk, they scatter in panic and retreat entirely from the district. The fairies' reluctance to face religious authority directly demonstrates their fear of the sacred and their ultimate powerlessness before the priest's spiritual authority. Dermod never encounters them again.

irish-003.title: The Legend of Knockgrafton
irish-003.lead: Lusmore, a hunchbacked craftsman, wanders the countryside despite his deformity.
irish-003.body_html: Lusmore, a hunchbacked craftsman, wanders the countryside despite his deformity. One evening, he hears fairies singing a melody that lacks a proper ending. Sitting nearby, Lusmore adds his own voice, completing the tune with a fitting conclusion. The fairies, delighted by his artistic contribution, reward him generously. When Lusmore wakes, he discovers his hump has vanished, his back is straight, and he is clothed in fine new garments. His deformity has been removed and his health restored. From that day forward, Lusmore lives as a healthy man, his gift for music and melody having earned him the fairies' magical blessing. The tale teaches that artistic talent and kindness to the supernatural brings unexpected rewards.

irish-004.title: Teig O'Kane and the Corpse
irish-004.lead: Teig O'Kane, a reckless young gambling man, encounters fairies one night who force him to carry a corpse through the darkness, traveling from churchyard to churchyard seeking burial.
irish-004.body_html: Teig O'Kane, a reckless young gambling man, encounters fairies one night who force him to carry a corpse through the darkness, traveling from churchyard to churchyard seeking burial. The corpse grows heavier with each step, and Teig finds no priest willing to receive it. Through the long night, Teig is tormented by the weight and his terror. By dawn, exhausted and chastened, Teig swears an oath to reform his ways. The fairies release him from this trial. From that day forward, Teig abandons gambling and drinking. He marries the woman he had wronged—a girl he had left pregnant—and becomes a devoted family man and respected member of his community. His supernatural punishment transforms him into a moral person, teaching that even the wicked can be redeemed through suffering.

japanese-001.title: My Lord Bag of Rice
japanese-001.lead: A samurai warrior named Fujiwara Hidesato encounters a dragon on a bridge who asks for help defeating a destructive centipede that has plagued him for years.
japanese-001.body_html: A samurai warrior named Fujiwara Hidesato encounters a dragon on a bridge who asks for help defeating a destructive centipede that has plagued him for years. The creature is enormous and invulnerable to normal weapons. Hidesato accepts the challenge, applying human saliva to an arrow—the one substance the centipede cannot resist. He fires the arrow true and slays the monster with a single shot. The grateful Dragon King appears and rewards the warrior with an inexhaustible bag of rice that never empties, no matter how much is taken from it. This magical gift makes Hidesato prosperous and wealthy for life, and he becomes known throughout the land as "My Lord Bag of Rice" for his greatest treasure.

japanese-002.title: The Tongue-Cut Sparrow
japanese-002.lead: An old man keeps a beloved pet sparrow that he cherishes deeply.
japanese-002.body_html: An old man keeps a beloved pet sparrow that he cherishes deeply. One day his cruel wife discovers the bird has eaten her paste for starching her clothes. In anger, she cuts out the sparrow's tongue and drives it away. The heartbroken old man searches the mountains for his lost companion. He discovers the sparrow living in a beautiful mansion hidden in the forest—it is actually a fairy in bird form. She welcomes him warmly and offers him a small, ornate box filled with treasures. He accepts gratefully and returns home. His greedy wife, learning of the treasure, forces him to reveal the location. She climbs the mountain and demands a box for herself. The fairies give her a large chest, which she carries home eagerly. When opened, it pours forth demons and misfortunes that plague her forever, while the old man and his treasure live in peace and plenty.

japanese-003.title: The Story of Urashima Taro, the Fisher Lad
japanese-003.lead: A kind young fisherman, Urashima Taro, rescues a tortoise entangled in nets and releases it to the sea.
japanese-003.body_html: A kind young fisherman, Urashima Taro, rescues a tortoise entangled in nets and releases it to the sea. The tortoise reveals itself as the daughter of the Dragon King and invites him to an underwater palace. Urashima descends with her to a magnificent crystal kingdom beneath the waves, where time moves differently and he marries the princess. They live in joy and splendor, though Urashima grows homesick and requests to return to his village. His bride gives him a magical box, warning him never to open it. Upon reaching shore, Urashima finds three hundred years have passed. Everyone he knew is dead, and his village is unrecognizable. Overwhelmed by grief and confusion, he opens the forbidden box. Instantly, he ages to great old age—three hundred years catch up with him in moments—and he dies, the price of his curiosity and broken promise.

japanese-004.title: The Farmer and the Badger
japanese-004.lead: A farmer captures a mischievous badger that has been stealing and causing trouble.
japanese-004.body_html: A farmer captures a mischievous badger that has been stealing and causing trouble. The badger, a shape-shifter, deceives the farmer's wife by disguising itself as a beautiful woman. Under this deception, the creature kills the farmer's wife and cooks her flesh. When a clever rabbit befriends the badger and discovers the terrible crime, he devises revenge. The rabbit tricks the badger with flaming grass, setting fire to it while it rests. Badly burned and fleeing, the badger is then tricked into a clay boat on the river, where the rabbit drowns it, drowning. The farmer, grieving his wife, is consoled by the rabbit's explanation of what happened. The farmer honors the rabbit as his savior, and the creature remains his companion for the rest of his life.
characteristics: Culture/Region: Japan

japanese-005.title: The Adventures of Kintaro, the Golden Boy
japanese-005.lead: A boy of superhuman strength is raised alone in the mountains by a wise woman.
japanese-005.body_html: A boy of superhuman strength is raised alone in the mountains by a wise woman. He grows up surrounded by wild animals—bears, deer, and monkeys—whom he befriends and masters through his incredible power. Kintaro plays games of strength with the animals, wrestling bears and lifting boulders as if they were toys. A disguised military general, traveling through the mountains, observes the boy's prowess and recognizes his extraordinary potential as a warrior. The general reveals himself and invites Kintaro to come down from the mountains to become a samurai. Kintaro accepts, leaving his animal companions behind. Through training and discipline, he becomes a legendary warrior and is eventually appointed chief of the "Four Braves," Japan's most celebrated military band. Later in life, his wealth and power allow him to rescue his mother from poverty, and they live together in honor and comfort.

amgothic-001.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow
amgothic-001.lead: In the secluded valley of Sleepy Hollow there taught a lanky schoolmaster named Ichabod Crane, a man of huge ears, a long nose, and an insatiable appetite, who set his sights on marrying Katrina Van Tassel, the wealthy farmer's daughter.
amgothic-001.body_html: In the secluded valley of Sleepy Hollow there taught a lanky schoolmaster named Ichabod Crane, a man of huge ears, a long nose, and an insatiable appetite, who set his sights on marrying Katrina Van Tassel, the wealthy farmer's daughter. But Ichabod had a rival for her hand, the roguish Brom Bones, and the valley itself was haunted by an old legend: the ghost of a Hessian trooper who had lost his head to a cannonball in the Revolutionary War, and who rode forth nightly on horseback in search of it, known to every fireside as the Headless Horseman. One autumn night, having been rejected by Katrina at a party, Ichabod rode home alone through the dark hollow and encountered a cloaked horseman waiting silently by the bridge. Terror seized him as the stranger spurred alongside, and Ichabod saw to his horror that the rider was headless, his head carried instead upon the pommel of his saddle. The horseman hurled the head straight at him, and Ichabod was struck down. He was never seen in the valley again; only his hat and a shattered pumpkin were found the next morning beside the brook.

amgothic-002.title: Young Goodman Brown
amgothic-002.lead: Young Goodman Brown set out from Salem village at sunset, turning back at his own threshold to kiss his young wife Faith farewell before keeping a secret appointment in the forest.
amgothic-002.body_html: Young Goodman Brown set out from Salem village at sunset, turning back at his own threshold to kiss his young wife Faith farewell before keeping a secret appointment in the forest. Deep among the trees he met a grave, elderly traveler carrying a black serpent-staff that seemed almost to writhe of its own accord, and this stranger led him onward toward a nameless purpose. As the night deepened, Brown pressed forward alone through the darkening wood until he came upon an open clearing, ringed by blazing pines, where a rock stood like an altar. There, gathered beneath the flames, he beheld the faces of his most respected neighbors: elders who sat upon the town council by day, and pious women who prayed devoutly every Sabbath, all assembled now for a communion of evil. Among the figures at the altar he glimpsed, or believed he glimpsed, his own wife Faith. Brown cried out in anguish, and in an instant found himself alone in the cold forest, uncertain whether it had been real or a dream — but from that night forward he could never again look upon his neighbors, his minister, or even his own wife without dark suspicion, and he lived out his days a stern, sad, distrustful man.

amgothic-003.title: The Tell-Tale Heart
amgothic-003.lead: An unnamed narrator lived with an old man whose only offense was a pale blue eye, filmed like that of a vulture, which the narrator grew to hate beyond reason.
amgothic-003.body_html: An unnamed narrator lived with an old man whose only offense was a pale blue eye, filmed like that of a vulture, which the narrator grew to hate beyond reason. For seven nights he crept silently into the old man's chamber to watch him sleep, until on the eighth night the man awoke in terror, and the narrator, hearing his victim's heart beating loud with fear, threw open his lantern and leaped upon him. The old man shrieked once, and the narrator smothered him beneath his own heavy bed, then dismembered the body and hid the pieces beneath the floorboards of the chamber, congratulating himself on a deed so cleverly concealed that no stain or sign remained. When police officers arrived to investigate a neighbor's report of a cry, the narrator calmly invited them in and sat them directly above the hidden corpse, answering their questions with easy confidence. But as the officers lingered in idle conversation, the narrator began to hear a low, dull, quickening sound rising from beneath the floor — the beating of the dead man's heart, growing louder in his ears until, driven past endurance, he shrieked out a full confession and ordered the officers to tear up the planks.

ausgothic-001.title: The Drover's Wife
ausgothic-001.lead: In a two-roomed timber house deep in the flat, monotonous bush, nineteen miles from the nearest sign of civilisation, a drover's wife was left alone with her four children while her husband was away droving sheep.
ausgothic-001.body_html: In a two-roomed timber house deep in the flat, monotonous bush, nineteen miles from the nearest sign of civilisation, a drover's wife was left alone with her four children while her husband was away droving sheep. One afternoon the children spotted a black snake slip beneath the floor of the house through a crack in the slabs, and the mother, unable to draw it out, resolved that none of them would sleep in the house that night. She made a bed for the children upon the kitchen table, brought in the dog, and sat down beside them with a stick in readiness, determined to keep watch until dawn. Through the long night a thunderstorm raged outside while she sewed and read by candlelight, glancing again and again at the wall where the dog watched a crack in the slabs, thinking over the hardships of her lonely bush life — fires fought alone, floods, a mad bullock, and a child she had once carried nineteen miles for help. Near daybreak the snake at last showed itself at the crack, and the dog seized it and beat it against the floor until it was dead. She lifted the mangled body on a stick, burned it in the fire, and watched it turn to ash. Her eldest boy, seeing tears in her eyes, threw his arms about her neck and vowed he would never leave her for the droving life, and she held him close as the pale morning light broke at last over the bush.

ausgothic-002.title: The Haunted Author
ausgothic-002.lead: A weary novelist, having worked long into the night at his desk, was startled by a visitor who forced his way into the study: a tall, scowling man in a rough coat, who claimed with bitter familiarity to be a villain the author himself had i
ausgothic-002.body_html: A weary novelist, having worked long into the night at his desk, was startled by a visitor who forced his way into the study: a tall, scowling man in a rough coat, who claimed with bitter familiarity to be a villain the author himself had invented and killed off in an earlier book. As the author protested, more and more of his own fictional creations began to appear before him — a poisoner, a ruined heiress, a string of tragic and wronged characters — each accusing him of the suffering he had written into their lives, until the study seemed to dissolve and he found himself surrounded by his own imagination at the edge of a precipice, his creations threatening to hurl him over in revenge for what he had made them suffer. Just as the mob of phantoms closed in around him, a servant's voice broke through the vision, bringing news from the printers, and the author woke with a start at his own desk, the whole nightmare having passed in the space of an exhausted doze. Shaken but resolved, he took up his pen once more and calmly sentenced his villain to a prison cell in the next chapter, reasserting his mastery over the creatures of his own making.
